paragraphs: This list is for self-questioning only and does not constitute recruitment criteria, a capability score, or a conclusion evaluating forestry and conservation work outcomes. This page is written according to the US O*NET-SOC 19-4071.00 'Forest and Conservation Technicians' (the fixed index gives this asset the Chinese name whose English rendering is 'Forest and conservation technicians'; the main objects are providing technical assistance for the conservation of soil and water resources and forests and related natural resources, possibly compiling data on forest tract size and composition and condition under the direction of foresters, or training and leading forestry workers in forest propagation and fire prevention and suppression, and possibly assisting conservation scientists in managing and improving rangelands and wildlife habitats).

Exercise prompt | a completely fictional resource survey and tending task. Write a survey and work scheduling draft: (1) how to select and establish sample plots to procedure and measure and record stand data with reviewable quality; (2) how to survey and map and enter data into databases for later analysis; (3) how to arrange tending work such as thinning and weeding and replanting and supervise work quality; (4) how to carry out patrol and fire use management and fire prevention outreach and record anomalies; (5) how to pause and report or refer to authorised personnel to procedure in situations such as severe weather and terrain, fire and fire use, chemical and equipment use, logging and contract boundary violations, and conflict with the public or contractors. Answer using public information and simulated data, and do not use any real forest land, institution or party information.

Fit signals | O*NET points of focus: face-to-face discussions with individuals and teams every day (98%), teamwork extremely important (87%), using email every day (82%), telephone conversations every day (67%), contact with others most of the time (51%), outdoors exposed to all weather once a week or more (56%), making decisions every day (57%), decision freedom considerable (53%), leading or coordinating others important (55%), very high responsibility for the health and safety of others (52%), wearing routine protective or safety equipment every day (51%), dealing with the external public extremely important (48%), walking or running more than half the time (47%). If you are willing to measure and record outdoors to procedure, can lead a crew in tending and fire prevention work and also handle public communication, the daily requirements of this occupation are closer to your way of working.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows: the consequences of error are serious (47%), exposed to very hot or very cold temperatures once a week or more (46%), exposed to minor burns or cuts or bites or stings once a month or more (45%), working in an uncontrolled indoor environment once a week or more (60%), in an enclosed vehicle or operating enclosed equipment once a week or more (48%), exposed to distracting noise every day (39%), exposed to contaminants once a month or more (37%), performing repetitive motions more than half the time (39%), bending or twisting the body about half the time (30%), dealing with unpleasant or discourteous people once a year or more (39%). Field work carries terrain and weather and wildlife and equipment risks, and survey and data errors affect resource decisions and contract execution. If you find it hard to bear long periods outdoors and physical load, or lack patience for field safety and accurate records, treat these as real costs that need careful weighing.

Taking on the judgement | real fit comes from being able to do three things in the same season: get the survey right (sample plot selection and measurement and records, mapping and database entry, reviewable data), lead the work well (arranging and supervising tending work such as thinning and weeding and replanting, patrol and fire use management and fire prevention outreach, and equipment and chemical and device safety), and take on reviewable compliance and supervision responsibility (assisting with permits and contracts and regulation enforcement, protecting resources and facilities, and reporting and referring anomalies and conflicts per procedure). It is suggested to test this through one verifiable experience (taking part in a sample plot survey and mapping and reviewing the data, following one tending or fire prevention operation and writing the work record, or completing a field safety and equipment use practical assessment), rather than relying only on the conclusion of an interest questionnaire.

Safety work sample (a completely fictional task pack): given the quarterly tasks for a completely fictional piece of forest land (including several sample plots, one forest compartment awaiting thinning and replanting, and one area requiring patrol and fire use management), complete a survey and work record draft within 90 minutes: the sample plot selection and measurement and record plan (number and location and diameter at breast height and tree height and regeneration and damage), the mapping and database entry plan, the work scheduling and quality supervision plan for thinning and weeding and replanting, the patrol and fire use management and fire prevention outreach and anomaly record plan, and the field safety and equipment and chemical use and conflict handling plan, stating clearly which situations require pausing and reporting to procedure or referral to authorised personnel (such as severe weather and terrain risk, fire and fire use anomalies, chemical and equipment accidents, logging and contract boundary violations, and conflict with the public or contractors).

Scope | O*NET19-4071 provides technical assistance for the conservation of soil, water, forests and related natural resources. Actual tasks may include thinning, leading crews, road planning, logging supervision, experiments, fire management, enforcing regulations and issuing fire / timber / forest use permits, and management, research, fire prevention or permit tasks cannot be excluded wholesale. The occupational description does not automatically confer licensing, enforcement or fireground command authority in China or any jurisdiction; verify by actual appointment, qualifications, institution and law.

entries: Resource survey and measurement | sample plots and stand data | select and measure sample plots and record stand area and composition and condition and regeneration and damage.
Mapping and data management | surveying and database entry | survey and map and enter and maintain databases for analysis and management use.
Tending and afforestation work | thinning and weeding and replanting | arrange and supervise thinning and weeding and replanting and tree propagation and nursery work.

Fire prevention and patrol | fire use management and fire prevention outreach | patrol and protect resources and facilities, carry out fire use management and fire prevention outreach and record anomalies.

Work supervision and compliance assistance | contracts and permits and regulations | assist in supervising logging and contracting work and assist in enforcing permits and resource protection regulations.

Training and crew leadership and public service | crew leadership and outreach and answering questions | train and lead forestry workers and provide forestry education and advice to forest owners and the public.

paragraphs:
Work context | the O*NET 19-4071.00 work context shows (the percentages are respondent distributions, not individual working hours or accident rates): the work is dominated by field survey and tending and patrol, with teamwork and outdoor conditions prominent.
Communication and collaboration | face-to-face discussions with individuals and teams every day (98%), teamwork extremely important (87%), using email every day (82%), telephone conversations every day (67%), contact with others most of the time (51%).

External contact and the public | dealing with external customers or the public extremely important (48%), dealing with unpleasant or angry or discourteous people at least once a year but not monthly (39%), conflict situations at least once a year but not monthly (44%).

Outdoors and environment | outdoors exposed to all weather at least once a week but not every day (56%), working in an uncontrolled indoor environment at least once a week but not every day (60%), exposed to very hot or very cold temperatures at least once a week but not every day (46%), in an enclosed vehicle or operating enclosed equipment at least once a week but not every day (48%), exposed to extremely bright or inadequate lighting at least once a week but not every day (24%).

Hazards and protection | wearing routine protective or safety equipment every day (51%), exposed to minor burns or cuts or bites or stings at least once a month but not every week (45%), exposed to contaminants at least once a month but not every week (37%), exposed to distracting noise every day (39%).

Decisions and impact | making decisions every day (57%), decision freedom considerable (53%), a very important impact of decisions on colleagues and unit results (50%), some freedom to determine tasks and priorities (38%), the consequences of error serious (47%).
Leadership and responsibility | leading or coordinating others important (55%), very high responsibility for the health and safety of others (52%), fairly high responsibility for the work results of others (29%).

Time and physical | a typical working week of 40 hours (53%), time pressure at least once a month but not every week (38%), standing about half the time (52%), walking or running more than half the time (47%), handling, controlling or feeling objects continually or almost continually (38%), performing repetitive motions more than half the time (39%), bending or twisting the body about half the time (30%).
Other conditions | precision or accuracy important (35% very important), repeating the same task important (32%), job competition medium (41%), writing letters and memos at least once a week but not every day (33%), a controlled indoor environment at least once a week but not every day (53%).

Environment and pace | O*NET respondents: 56% are outdoors in all weather at least once a week but not every day, 60% are indoors uncontrolled at that frequency, 46% experience hot and cold temperatures at that frequency, and 48% are in an enclosed vehicle at that frequency; 39% have noise every day, 53% have a typical working week of 40 hours with 47% more than 40 hours, and 38% experience time pressure at least once a month but not every week. 47% walk more than half the time, 52% stand about half the time, and 39% perform repetitive motions more than half the time; these are respondent distributions, not individual working hours or a medium-to-high physical rating. Seasonal / irregular / regular arrangement answers are 15 / 32 / 53%, so it cannot be said that most work in the field every day or that summer is uniformly the busiest; the specific fire season, duty accommodation and load are verified by position.

Tools and materials | equipment: tree measurement and survey instruments (diameter tape, hypsometer, quadrat and tape measure, GPS and compass), surveying and mapping and database software and drones, field vehicles and all-terrain vehicles, fire prevention and suppression equipment and communication devices, nursery and tending and weeding tools, equipment and chemical application equipment, and protective equipment (helmet, goggles, gloves, protective clothing and non-slip boots). Materials: seedlings and seeds and substrate, chemicals for weeding and pest and disease control (stored and applied to procedure), and marking and archive materials. Documents: forest stand maps and management and work design documents, sample plot and survey record sheets, permit and contract texts, work and safety procedures, and fire prevention and emergency processes. Drones are a newly added task and are not commonly used or required in all positions; all chemical use and management and enforcement judgements are subject to the valid version of the procedures and regulations.

Select and establish sample plots and measure → record and map and enter data → arrange tending and replanting work → lead the crew and supervise quality → patrol and fire use management and outreach → record and report and hand over

Quality suggestion | check methods, original records, maps and anomalies against the applicable survey, work, acceptance and safety procedures. Management, experimentation, fire management and permitting may be O*NET tasks, but the real scope must be verified against the appointment and jurisdiction. On finding a personal threat, take safety evasive action first and call the police and report, without waiting for approval before withdrawing; non-urgent design and permit changes follow the real procedure.

Responsibility comparison | forestry professionals focus more on forest management plans, harvesting methods and contracts; conservation scientists focus on soil and water conservation and management plans and actually implement and supervise projects. This occupation may also take part in planning, permitting, fire management, experiments and public advice; compare by specific tasks and appointment and do not draw exclusionary boundaries from titles.

Boundary review points | pause and escalate when the following arise: severe weather and terrain or flood and landslide risk; fire and fire use anomalies or an incipient fire; chemical and equipment accidents or personnel injury; logging and contracting work overstepping boundaries or violating permits and work design; major inconsistencies in data and mapping; and conflict or threats with the public or contractors. These are handled by the forestry and conservation lead, the fire prevention and safety lead and the competent authority per regulations and procedures.
Measure sample plots → record and map → arrange tending → lead the crew and supervise → patrol and outreach → record and report

Comparison | forestry and conservation workers may also assist with surveys and GIS maps, so they are not limited to manual execution; this occupation focuses more on technical assistance, data, supervision and crew leadership, and the tasks overlap, so verify by actual position and authority.

This occupation may also take part in planning, permitting, fire management, experiments and public advice; compare by specific tasks and appointment and do not draw exclusionary boundaries from titles.

Responsibility comparison | forestry professionals focus more on forest management plans, harvesting methods and contracts; conservation scientists focus on soil and water conservation and management plans and actually implement and supervise projects. This occupation may also take part in planning, permitting, fire management, experiments and public advice; compare by specific tasks and appointment and do not draw exclusionary boundaries from titles.

Difference from environmental-science-and-protection-technicians and forest-fire-inspectors-and-prevention-specialists: the former focus on sampling and monitoring environmental media and identifying pollution; the latter focus on fire prevention inspection and prevention and fire cause investigation; this occupation centres on the survey and tending and patrol and work supervision of stands and soil and water resources and habitat.

Before choosing this occupation, compare: the real tasks (the share of field survey and mapping and work supervision and patrol and outreach), qualification and training paths (relevant degree or certificate and internship and field safety and equipment training), working conditions and responsibility (seasonal and fire season duty, outdoor and equipment risk, crew leadership and safety responsibility), and growth paths (technician, specialist and crew leader positions, forestry and conservation scientist direction, or supervisory positions). Employers vary considerably (federal and state and local forestry and protected area agencies, consulting and logging companies, nurseries and non-profit organisations) and this should be verified against actual recruitment and on-site experience.

Responsibility comparison | forestry professionals focus more on forest management plans, harvesting methods and contracts; conservation scientists focus on soil and water conservation and management plans and actually implement and supervise projects. This occupation may also take part in planning, permitting, fire management, experiments and public advice; compare by specific tasks and appointment and do not draw exclusionary boundaries from titles.

AI task exposure | digital tools may assist with remote sensing and image interpretation and stand mapping, sample plot data entry and statistics, drone patrol and imagery and initial screening for growth and damage identification, database and archive search, and drafting reports and outreach materials. But field measurement and records, work scheduling and quality supervision, patrol and fire use management and on-site safety and conflict handling remain with technicians and crew leaders; task exposure does not equal job replacement, and tool outputs cannot replace field verification.

Adoption conditions | digital tools entering survey and work processes need to satisfy: tool outputs are traceable and reviewable and do not replace judgement about stand data and work quality and safety; remote sensing and imagery and automatic identification results must be field-verified and manually confirmed before being used for management and reporting; steps involving permits and contracts and enforcement assistance and chemical use must not be completed automatically by tools. A technology demonstration does not mean the institution has adopted it, nor does it change work and safety and regulatory responsibility.

Data and system thresholds | before adoption, verify: whether sample plot and remote sensing data can be traced back to method and equipment and personnel and time; whether coordinates and projections and patches and database definitions are consistent; the permissions and retention periods for imagery and maps and photographs; the data consistency and audit trails with management and permit and archive systems; and whether offline field work with original records retained is possible during network or equipment failure.

Human control points and manual review | sample plot selection and measurement and records, work scheduling and quality supervision, patrol and fire use management and on-site safety, chemical and equipment use, permit and contract and enforcement assistance, and conflict and accident handling must be completed by technicians and crew leaders; any remote sensing interpretation, automatic identification, statistics or report draft generated by a tool must be manually checked with a trace left before use.

Residual responsibility | matters that must not be released automatically: whether the data reflect the real stand condition, whether the work was completed to design and meets quality standards, whether fire use and chemical and equipment use are safe and compliant, whether there is any boundary violation or permit breach, and decisions involving stopping work and reporting. No tool output equals a work conclusion or an authorisation decision.

Failure risk | unreviewed tool outputs may cause patch and data errors, inaccurate work scheduling, missed patrol and hazards, image misjudgements treated as actual conditions, and distorted records and archives, creating resource loss and safety and compliance risk. Before deployment, make clear who reviews and against what original data and field verification.

Employment evidence boundaries | the employment and wage data of this occupation must be distinguished by definition: the US figures from O*NET and the BLS are estimates under a specific statistical definition and cannot be extrapolated directly to mainland China or other regions; China uses industry category average wages as a background proxy, which does not constitute an occupational wage conclusion. Anything generated should be traceable back to the original inputs and sources, and fluent wording must not be treated as correct evidence.

Practical response | first put digital tools into low-risk steps that can be rolled back and audited (sample plot data entry and statistics, remote sensing and mapping drafts, archive search, drafting reports and outreach materials), subject to confirmation by technicians and crew leaders and to field verification; decide whether to expand the scope of use based on error and accident records, and always keep manual confirmation for work and safety and compliance judgements.

Cross-market definition boundaries | mainland China and the United States have different industry and occupational classification systems: mainland China publishes the average wage of employed persons in urban units by national economic industry category, without listing this occupation separately; the United States gives estimates by SOC occupation and industry. The two cannot be spliced or converted, and industry averages cannot replace occupational wages.

Insufficient evidence: mainland China has not established public occupational wage statistics precisely corresponding to 'forest and conservation technicians'; industry averages, recruitment quotes or third-party estimates are not used as substitutes.

Mainland China wage evidence review points | this page provides only statistical definitions, industry background proxies and a register of visible gaps, and does not provide an estimated wage for this occupation. Before using any figure, first confirm whether its statistical definition (industry category / occupation), statistical period, unit of measurement and covered population are comparable with this occupation.

US wage evidence review points | the US figures on this page come from BLS OEWS May 2025 and the BLS 2025—2035 employment projections (some presented via O*NET). Before use, confirm their occupational scope (SOC 19-4071), whether they include overtime and seasonal employment and benefits (OEWS excludes benefits), and whether they are national rather than a single region or institution.

Mainland China wage evidence — market definition | the National Bureau of Statistics publishes the average wage of employed persons in urban units by industry category, which is a national urban unit definition and is not split by occupation; the average wages of related categories such as agriculture, forestry, animal husbandry and fishery can only serve as background reference and cannot replace occupational wages. Employment forms in forestry and conservation positions (established posts, public welfare posts, labour dispatch and seasonal work) vary considerably and are hard for public statistics to cover.

Insufficient evidence: no occupational wage median for forest and conservation technicians that can be verified by occupation was obtained for mainland China; industry category averages are not used as substitutes.

Mainland China wage evidence — statistical period | industry average wages are an annual definition (the figures below are for 2025, published in 2026), which differs from the US May 2025 point-in-time wage on this page, and the two periods cannot be mixed.

Cross-market definition boundaries | mainland China industry average wages and US occupational wages differ in statistical object, period and definition; this page presents them separately with their limitations noted, does not perform currency conversion, and does not treat industry averages as occupational wages.

Mainland China wage evidence — unit of measurement | the National Bureau of Statistics publishes annual average wages in 'yuan / year' on a pre-tax total wage definition (including personal income tax withheld by the employer and the employee's own social insurance and housing provident fund contributions); US OEWS publishes in 'US dollars / hour' or 'US dollars / year', excluding overtime and bonuses and benefits. The units and inclusions differ and cannot be compared directly.

Insufficient evidence: no forest and conservation technician wage data verifiable by region or employment form was obtained for mainland China; individual quotes or second-hand accounts are not used as substitutes.

Mainland China wage evidence — covered population | the urban non-private unit definition covers employed persons in non-private legal entities in urban areas, and the urban private unit definition covers employed persons in private units; neither covers sole proprietors, the self-employed or casual labour; established posts and public welfare posts and seasonal and labour dispatch employment in forestry and conservation positions vary considerably and are hard for public statistics to cover.

US wage evidence — market definition | BLS OEWS is a sample survey estimate representing wages reported by employers; it excludes the self-employed and the full income of some seasonal positions. The median represents the midpoint of the distribution and is not a starting wage, nor does it represent any single institution or region.

US wage evidence — statistical period | the wage is May 2025 OEWS; employment and growth are from the 2025—2035 employment projections (openings are additionally referenced from the 2024—2034 annual average presented by O*NET). The two types of data have different reference points and must not be mixed into a conclusion for the same point in time.

US wage evidence — unit of measurement | published in 'US dollars / hour' and 'US dollars / year'; the annual average wage is converted on a full-year full-time basis, seasonal employment and overtime and allowances are not included, and the converted value does not equal personal actual income.

US wage evidence — covered population | covers employed persons reported by non-farm establishment employers and excludes the self-employed and short-term seasonal work; positions in federal and state and local agencies and consulting and logging companies differ considerably in allowances and seasonal structure, and public statistics can hardly cover them completely.

US wage evidence — occupational scope | the figures on this page correspond to SOC 19-4071 (Forest and Conservation Technicians); they exclude forest and conservation workers (45-4011), foresters (19-1032), conservation scientists (19-1031), forest fire inspectors and prevention specialists (33-2022), environmental science and protection technicians (19-4042), fish and game wardens (33-3031), first-line supervisors of farming fishing and forestry workers (45-1011) and agricultural technicians (19-4011). Wages across occupations must not be mixed.

US wage evidence — sampling and missing data limitations | OEWS is a sample estimate with sampling error, and estimates may be missing or unreliable at industry and regional detail; this occupation has a medium employment size (about 33,800 people in 2024, BLS occupational projection base period, presented via O*NET; about 30,410 people under the OEWS May 2025 presentation; about 32,800 people in the BLS 2025—2035 base period), but industry and regional detail may still be missing; this page obtained no industry-readable industry wage median, and that position is registered as a visible gap; industry averages or third-party estimates are not used as substitutes.

paragraphs: Conclusion | the core difference between this occupation and adjacent occupations is 'authority and outputs': this occupation carries the technical and execution responsibility for survey and measurement and mapping and work scheduling and supervision and crew leadership and outreach; forest and conservation workers carry out physical and work tasks under direction; foresters are responsible for stand management and harvesting and long-term planning; conservation scientists are responsible for scientific research and management plans; forest fire inspectors and prevention specialists are responsible for fire prevention inspection and prevention and fire cause investigation; environmental science and protection technicians are responsible for environmental sampling and monitoring. Authority and outputs differ, and judgement and sign-off authority cannot be carried across positions.

Evidence note | the comparison objects in the table below come from the O*NET occupational classification and publicly available materials on sale, and are used to help distinguish the work content of adjacent occupations and choose a fit; they do not constitute qualification, recruitment or compensation conclusions. The wages and employment of each occupation must be verified separately under their own SOC definitions, and this table does not compare figures or treat one occupation's wage as a proxy for another's.

Preface | the following comparison is laid out in four columns: 'occupational direction — core work and outputs — key differences — what it is a better choice for'. Forestry and natural resource field positions are often linked by season and operation, but linkage does not equal substitutability; when choosing across directions, the procedures, regulations and safety and qualification requirements must be relearned.

Centred on the survey and tending and patrol and work supervision of stands and soil and water resources and habitat: sample plot selection and measurement and records, mapping and database entry, scheduling and quality supervision of thinning and weeding and replanting, patrol and fire use management and fire prevention outreach, and crew leadership and public outreach.
Better suited to people willing to survey and record outdoors to procedure over the long term, who can lead a crew in tending and fire prevention work and also handle public communication.

Output is usable resource data and work results: sample plot and survey records, stand maps and mapping and databases, work and acceptance records for tending and replanting, and patrol and fire prevention outreach and anomaly records.
This occupation: forest and conservation technicians

Centred on carrying out forestry and conservation physical and work tasks under direction: planting and thinning and weeding seedlings, facility and road maintenance, and fire prevention and suppression work and equipment carrying.
Better suited to people who carry out physical and work tasks under on-site direction; those who prefer survey and mapping and technical coordination fit this occupation.
Output is completed work tasks: planting and tending and clearing records, facility and road maintenance records, and firefighting and equipment use records.
Forest and Conservation Workers
Centred on stand management and harvesting and long-term planning: management plans and harvest design, stand growth and regeneration and benefit analysis, and management and permitting decisions.

Better suited to people who take on management and harvest decisions and professional responsibility; this occupation compiles and analyses data under their direction and assists with execution and supervision.
Output is management and harvest plans: management and work design documents, stand growth and benefit analysis, and harvesting and regeneration and acceptance conclusions.
Foresters

Centred on scientific research and management plans for natural resources and ecosystems: ecological and resource survey and modelling, conservation and restoration plan design, and monitoring and evaluation and publication.
Better suited to people who take on research and plan design responsibility; this occupation provides survey data and execution and supervision support.
Output is research and plan results: survey and modelling and monitoring results, restoration and management plans, and evaluation and publication.
Conservation Scientists

Centred on fire prevention inspection and prevention and fire cause investigation: fuel and facility and fire use inspection, fire prevention outreach and prevention plans, and fire cause investigation and reporting.

Better suited to people whose professional direction is fire prevention inspection and prevention and fire cause investigation; this occupation focuses on survey and tending and patrol and carries out part of the fire prevention outreach.
Output is fire prevention inspection and prevention conclusions: inspection and hazard rectification records, fire prevention outreach and plan documents, and fire cause investigation and reports.
Forest Fire Inspectors and Prevention Specialists

Centred on sampling and monitoring environmental media and identifying pollution: sampling and analysis of water and soil and air and biological samples, monitoring networks and data management, and environmental impact and pollution identification.
Better suited to people whose focus is environmental sampling and monitoring and pollution identification; this occupation focuses on survey and tending and patrol of stands and habitat.
Output is environmental monitoring results: sampling and analysis records, monitoring data and reports, and pollution identification and rectification suggestions.
Environmental Science and Protection Technicians

Transition | this page sets adjacent positions side by side by 'authority and outputs', to help you judge which kind of forestry and natural resource field you want to invest in long term. Whichever direction you choose, what really determines whether you can take up the work is your understanding of procedures and regulations and safety requirements, your ability to stay accurate and reviewable in outdoor and equipment environments, and passing institutional and employer internship and assessment; an interest questionnaire is only for raising questions.

entries.answer: According to O*NET-SOC 19-4071.00, this occupation provides technical assistance for the conservation of soil and water resources and forests and related natural resources, and may compile and organise data on forest tract size and composition and condition under the direction of foresters, or train and lead forestry workers in forest propagation and fire prevention and suppression, and may assist conservation scientists in managing and improving rangelands and wildlife habitats. The work includes sample plot selection and measurement and records, mapping and database entry, arranging and supervising tending work such as thinning and weeding and replanting, patrol and fire use management and fire prevention outreach, assisting in enforcing permits and resource protection regulations, and providing forestry education and advice to forest owners and the public. It does not include stand management and harvest and long-term planning decisions, scientific research and plan formulation, logging and log transport machinery operation, fireground command, or the final determination of permits and enforcement and legal application.
entries.question: What does this occupation actually do?

entries.answer: Forest and conservation workers carry out planting and thinning and weeding and facility maintenance and other physical and work tasks under direction; foresters are responsible for stand management and harvesting and long-term planning and bear professional decision responsibility; conservation scientists are responsible for scientific research and management plans for natural resources and ecosystems; forest fire inspectors and prevention specialists are responsible for fire prevention inspection and prevention and fire cause investigation; environmental science and protection technicians are responsible for sampling and monitoring environmental media; fish and game wardens are responsible for enforcement and patrol. This occupation carries the technical and execution responsibility for survey and mapping and work scheduling and supervision and crew leadership and outreach.

entries.answer: In 2025 the median annual wage is 54,560 US dollars (median hourly wage 26.23 US dollars); percentiles are 40,330 / 47,360 / 68,600 / 83,630 US dollars per year; 2025 employment is about 32,800 people (BLS employment projection base period); it is projected to decline over 2025—2035 (about -2%), with about 3,900 average annual job openings (the 2024—2034 annual average presented by O*NET, including replacement needs). The OEWS May 2025 presentation shows about 30,410 people employed and the O*NET presentation shows about 33,800 people in 2024, with different base periods and definitions. The above uses the US definition and does not apply to other jurisdictions; OEWS excludes benefits and overtime and seasonal income.

entries.answer: Mainland China has not established public occupational wage statistics precisely corresponding to this occupation. The National Bureau of Statistics publishes the average wage of employed persons in urban units by industry category (for example agriculture, forestry, animal husbandry and fishery: urban non-private 74,424 yuan / year and urban private 46,552 yuan / year), which is an industry definition that does not distinguish occupations and can only serve as a background proxy; the mainland China part of this page retains the visible 'Insufficient evidence:' marker and does not use industry averages, recruitment quotes or third-party estimates as substitutes.

entries.answer: The O*NET work context shows: face-to-face discussion with individuals and teams every day 98%, teamwork extremely important 87%, using email every day 82%, outdoor exposure to all weather once a week or more 56%, working in an uncontrolled indoor environment once a week or more 60%, exposed to very hot or very cold temperatures once a week or more 46%, wearing protective equipment every day 51%, exposed to minor burns or cuts or bites or stings once a month or more 45%, walking or running more than half the time 47%, standing about half the time 52%, and the consequences of error serious 47%. Protective equipment and sensible scheduling and physical conditioning can reduce the risk, but field and equipment and weather risk and seasonal intensity are real costs.
entries.question: What are the work environment and physical requirements like?

entries.answer: The impact is mainly in the record and mapping and imagery and tabulation steps: remote sensing and image interpretation drafts, sample plot data entry and statistics, drone patrol and image organisation, GIS and mapping and databases, and drafting reports and outreach materials can be assisted by tools; sample plot selection and field measurement and field verification, work scheduling and quality supervision, patrol and fire use management and on-site safety, chemical and equipment use, and permit and contract and enforcement assistance remain with technicians and crew leaders. Task exposure does not equal job replacement, and tool outputs cannot replace field verification.
entries.question: Will AI affect this occupation?

entries.answer: O*NET shows that among new hires 35% have high school or equivalent education, 35% an associate or two-year qualification and 14% a bachelor's degree (84% in total), and the Job Zone is 3 (SVP 6.0 to <7.0); the BLS states that the typical entry education is an associate degree. In addition, on-the-job training and certificates are usually required in field safety and first aid and equipment and fire prevention and chemicals and surveying. Actual requirements are subject to the employer and position requirements and local rules.
entries.question: What education and training are required?

entries.answer: 'Having been trained', 'obtaining a degree or certificate', 'obtaining a chemical or fire prevention credential' and 'obtaining institutional authorisation' are four different states. A relevant degree or certificate and field safety and first aid and fire prevention and chemical and surveying training are common; using weeding and pest and disease control chemicals may require the corresponding credential under local regulations; taking part in patrol and enforcement assistance may involve additional background verification and position training. The preparation items listed on this page do not constitute a formal qualification list of any body.
entries.question: Are certificates or qualifications required?

entries.answer: Common failures include: steep and slippery terrain and severe weather and equipment and vehicle accidents, fire use and ignition and fire risk, errors in measurement and mapping and work design execution and acceptance, boundary violations or permit breaches and conflict with the public or contractors, improper storage and application and maintenance of chemicals and equipment, and health effects from long periods of field work and carrying and repetitive motion. Control points are acting per procedure and work design with records and pausing and withdrawing and reporting and referring per procedure; matters involving fire and boundary violations and enforcement and accidents are handled by the lead and the competent authority.

entries.answer: Under the US definition it is projected to decline over 2025—2035 (about -2%), with openings mainly from replacement needs; a projection is not an individual opportunity, and actual opportunities depend on local forestry and conservation investment and seasonal employment and mechanisation levels. You can move to adjacent positions such as forest and conservation workers, foresters, conservation scientists, forest fire inspection and prevention, environmental monitoring, fish and game enforcement, first-line farming fishing and forestry supervision and agricultural technician (which require relearning procedures and education and qualification requirements), or to technical management and training positions.

subject.summary: Forest And Conservation Technicians (O*NET-SOC 19-4071.00) provide technical assistance for the conservation of soil, water, forests and related natural resources: they may, under the direction of foresters, compile and organise data on the size, composition and condition of forest tracts, or train and lead forest workers in forest propagation and fire prevention and suppression, and assist conservation scientists in managing and improving rangelands and wildlife habitats. Official definition text: Provide technical assistance regarding the conservation of soil, water, forests, or related natural resources. May compile data pertaining to size, content, condition, and other characteristics of forest tracts under the direction of foresters, or train and lead forest workers in forest propagation and fire prevention and suppression. May assist conservation scientists in managing, improving, and protecting rangelands and wildlife habitats.
